title: What "no added sugar" is allowed to mean
standfirst: Some words on a pack have a legal meaning. Others are just nice words.

spans.text: The front of a pack is designed. The back of it is regulated. That gap is where most of the confusion lives.

A short list of words has a legal definition in the US, and a food has to meet it before the word can appear. "Free", "low", "reduced" and "light" all sit on that list, and each one names a threshold.
So "low sodium" is a measurement someone had to pass. It is not a mood.
Everything else on the front is marketing, and marketing is allowed to be true and misleading at the same time.
"No added sugar" means nobody stirred sugar in. It says nothing about how much sugar is in the food already, which for a fruit juice can be a great deal.
"Made with real fruit" sets no floor on how much. "Natural" has no agreed meaning for most foods. Neither word is a lie. Neither is a measurement.
Why the front works on us anyway

A claim on the front changes how people judge the whole food, including the parts the claim says nothing about. Researchers call it a halo, and it holds even when the panel on the back is right there.
That is not a failure of attention. It is what a well-designed pack is for.
Read the panel first and the front second. The panel is the part someone had to defend.
